soils developed on the upper slopes of the catchment have a limited capacity for sulphate adsorption, whereas soils developed on the lower slopes have a greater adsorption capacity.

the fate of sulphur and the role that soils play in modifying the chemistry of drainage water.
the role of soil sulphur transformations in the production and modification of sulphate-rich drainage water.

the sulphate adsorption characteristics of the lower slopes of the catchment are more than adequate to prevent significant sulphate leaching to surface waters, and that the soils of the upper slopes are not a significant source of sulphate to surface waters.

the sulphate retention capacity of upland soils is a function of both soil type and slope position, with soils of higher pH and lower organic matter content being more effective in sulphate retention.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the capacity of soils in the study area to retain sulphate is related to the soil's ability to retain cations, particularly Ca and Al.
sulphur retention in the upper slope soils is low and sulphate is likely to be transported in solution to the lower slope soils where it may be adsorbed.
the soils of lower slopes are more important in determining the sulphate content of surface water than those of upper slopes.

the capacity of upland soils to retain sulphates varies with soil type, and that this has important implications for the management of upland watersheds.
